Where it began

Vinod Kambli was born in Mumbai on 18 January 1972, into a Maharashtrian family whose roots lay in Bhadakambe, near Sakharpa in Ratnagiri. He learned the game under the coach Ramakant Achrekar, alongside a boy who became his close friend: Sachin Tendulkar.

The two of them announced themselves early. In a school match against St. Xavier's, Fort, they put on 664 together without being parted, Kambli's share an unbeaten 349, until Achrekar made them declare. Kambli then went out and took six for 37 with the ball. When he reached the Ranji Trophy for Mumbai, he hit the very first ball he faced for six.

The player

He first played for India in a one-day match against Pakistan in Sharjah in 1991, while a teenager, and his Test debut followed in 1993. What came next was remarkable. In his third Test, against England at the Wankhede Stadium, he made 224. In the next, against Zimbabwe, he made 227. Then came 125 and 120 against Sri Lanka, which made him the only man to score hundreds in three Tests in a row against three different countries. He reached 1,000 Test runs in just 14 innings, quicker than any Indian before him.

Across 17 Tests from 1993 to 1995 he made 1,084 runs at 54.20, with four hundreds, two of them doubles. By 2025 no Indian had finished a Test career with a better average, not even his friend Tendulkar.

A talent for every format

He was just as much at home in coloured clothing. In 1993 at Jaipur he made 100 not out against England on his 21st birthday, the first man to score a one-day international hundred on his birthday. He played in the World Cups of 1992 and 1996, and at the second of them made 106 against Zimbabwe at Kanpur. He was also in the squad that reached the final of the 2000 Champions Trophy.

His one curiosity was a liking for batting first. In his first innings of a Test he averaged 69.13; in the second, a modest 9.40. Perhaps he simply did his best work while the pitch was fresh.

What might have been

His last Test came in 1995, when he was only 23, and his last one-day international in 2000. By then he had shown the strokes and the appetite for huge scores that great batters are made of. Given a longer run, and the patient guidance young talent often needs, he had every gift to become one of the finest batters India has produced.

Away from the middle

He also turned out for Boland in South Africa's domestic game, and he retired from first-class cricket in 2011. He turned to coaching, opening his own academy in Mumbai, running the Mumbai Cricket Association's academy at BKC and from 2018 to 2022 serving as head coach of the Tendulkar Middlesex Global Academy. On television he became a familiar commentator, and even took to the screen as an actor, with a supporting part in the Kannada film Bettanagere.
